incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are stealing his identity to defraud vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using AI-generated images and videos of Leal, falsely offering immigration services such as US residency assistance for cash payments of around $2,200. The problem has escalated dramatically in recent months, with scammers directing potential victims through WhatsApp to send money via payment apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App.

After first noticing suspicious activity last October, the situation spiraled out of control over the past three months when potential clients began calling his office. Leal hired an anti-piracy company that has helped remove nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. He has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams. Leal is warning immigrants to verify anyone offering legal services online and to be cautious of social media advertisements promising immigration benefits.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has surfaced as part of a growing wave of AI-generated investment scams. The fabricated article claimed Bullock stormed out of an interview with Kohler over questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that such scams are becoming increasingly common and sophisticated, using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to appear legitimate.

ASIC's new research reveals dramatic increases in fraud activity, with the regulator taking down 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms rose 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most commonly impersonated figure, followed by other politicians and business leaders like Alan Kohler. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, the smart ring company valued at 11 billion dollars, of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The suit seeks class action status and alleges that Oura's rings, priced at 300 dollars and up, cannot accurately measure sleep stages as claimed. According to the lawsuit, Oura's algorithms and sensors lack the ability to detect the physiological signals needed for accurate sleep stage measurement, instead relying on AI-generated guesses that are no better than random chance.

The lawsuit specifically challenges Oura's marketing claims of 95 percent sleep staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs, arguing that genuine sleep labs use complex equipment including multiple electrodes to measure brain activity, which Oura rings do not have. Oura responded by standing behind its science and stating that its sleep staging has been validated through peer-reviewed studies against polysomnography, the gold standard for sleep measurement. The company noted that while its ring is not a medical device, it uses multiple physiological signals including heart rate and temperature to estimate sleep stages. It remains unclear at this early stage whether ring buyers could join the lawsuit or what compensation they might receive.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is abusing an AI tool called Cursor Agent for exploitation. Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, the group used Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet to conduct hands-on attacks against ten target organizations. The ransomware encrypts files using ChaCha20 encryption and includes a special ESXi mode that kills virtual machines to access their files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands.

The attackers also created custom tools to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. A second group of Aurora operators was identified using different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to S3 storage. Eight victim organizations across multiple countries were affected by this second cluster. Gambit published indicators of compromise and technical details to help organizations identify and defend against these attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee has filed a lawsuit claiming that Pizza Hut's artificial intelligence-powered delivery system called Dragontail caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across five northeastern states, alleges the system created cascading operational problems and customer dissatisfaction after its rollout in 2024. The franchisee says the platform gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations, causing drivers to wait up to fifteen minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering pizzas immediately, resulting in late arrivals and spoiled food quality.

Before Dragontail's implementation, Chaac reported that over 90 percent of deliveries arrived within 30 minutes and the company achieved double-digit sales growth. After the rollout, the franchisee experienced sharp performance declines, with year-over-year sales in New York City swinging from positive 10.19 percent to negative 9.78 percent. The lawsuit, filed in May in Texas Business Court, claims Pizza Hut failed to adequately train operators and ignored worsening delivery metrics despite the franchisee's complaints. Chaac is seeking over $100 million in damages plus attorney's fees. Pizza Hut declined to comment beyond stating it would respond through legal channels.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to deceive public figures into paying fees for supposed interview opportunities. Authors, entertainers and other professionals have received highly personalized emails claiming to offer spots on the popular NPR show, complete with detailed references to their work and professional-looking booking procedures. One victim, a history professor at Misericordia University, initially believed the invitation was legitimate before being asked to pay $250 for production costs. She became suspicious when Gross supposedly handled logistics personally, which seemed unusual for such a major production.

WHYY, NPR and law enforcement are investigating the scam, which experts attribute to artificial intelligence making fraudulent impersonations cheaper and more convincing than ever before. Similar schemes have targeted comedians and journalists like Nikki Glaser, Amy Poehler and Katie Couric. WHYY clarified that it never charges guests for interviews and stated that any request for payment should be considered fraudulent. Red flags include payment requests and suspicious email addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com, and potential victims should verify requests directly with the organization.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fake American research institute called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days with the goal of influencing artificial intelligence chatbots to promote pro-Israel arguments. The institute, which has no legal existence, physical address, or named staff, created content addressing controversial topics like Israeli war crimes and Gaza casualties by presenting Israel's perspective as neutral research. The operation used a specialized platform designed to optimize content so that AI systems would cite it, and was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as foreign agent material distributed on behalf of Israel.

The broader campaign involves tens of millions of dollars routed through European advertising company Havas Media and multiple American contractors, including a separate network run by former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale that has already influenced chatbot training data. Israeli officials have reportedly expressed frustration about the campaign's effectiveness despite substantial spending, with American public opinion polls showing declining support for Israel. Researchers note that while these efforts successfully influence AI outputs, they have not changed broader American public opinion, suggesting the underlying policy issues rather than messaging failures are driving the shift in sentiment.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim the companies scraped massive amounts of music from famous artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others. The record labels argue this represents willful copyright infringement on a massive scale and that the companies have been deliberately hiding which songs they used for training.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated that they could recreate famous copyrighted songs by using specific prompts in both AI generators. For example, they generated outputs resembling Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," Bill Haley's style, and an nearly identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits, filed in New York and Massachusetts, include a thumb drive of AI-generated music as evidence and represent a major legal battle over how generative AI services can use copyrighted material for training purposes.

incidents.title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio
incidents.summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements that resolve claims the company used copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. UMG had accused Udio of using hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar melodies without permission or compensation. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream and share their creations. Artists can opt into the platform and will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label and reflects the ongoing tension between AI companies and the entertainment industry. Founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, Udio has attracted millions of users since launching. The company's backers include music artist will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, signaling the music industry's evolving approach to embracing AI technology while protecting copyrights.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit involving a home damaged by fire have apologized for submitting court documents containing artificial intelligence-generated fake cases, false quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, filed suit in July 2024 after a 2020 fire in her Carson home made it uninhabitable. Following contractor repairs and storm damage, State Farm allegedly delayed approving additional work, leaving the home unfinished. Meni-Siliga and her husband exhausted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. The case proceeds to trial in October 2025.

State Farm lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to help prepare filings, incorrectly believing it performed accuracy checks through her firm's legal research subscription. She confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the errors and stated the firm updated its AI policy. State Farm said it expects external counsel to maintain the highest ethical standards. This incident reflects broader concerns as 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI, with a Paris-based researcher documenting nearly 1,900 legal hallucination cases worldwide.

stories.Headline: Who Writes AI's Rules When Someone Else Owns the Machines?
stories.Summary:
# Summary

South Africa withdrew its Draft National AI Policy in April 2026 after discovering that at least six of its 67 academic references were fabricated, highlighting a broader challenge facing the Global South. The incident underscores a critical debate about who controls artificial intelligence governance and infrastructure. Currently, the United States and China host roughly 86% of global data centre capacity, giving them power to set rules and prices for AI systems worldwide. This concentration of computing power represents what critics call "tech colonialism," where developing nations provide data and demand but lack ownership and control over the technology itself.

BRICS countries and other Global South nations are attempting to shift AI governance away from Western-led standards by emphasizing digital sovereignty and development rights. They are seeking to anchor AI governance within the United Nations rather than OECD-led bodies and have established organizations like the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. However, meaningful sovereignty requires owning physical infrastructure, not just adopting policies. The article notes that until developing nations build regional computing capacity and chip manufacturing capabilities, they remain dependent on foreign platforms controlled by American hyperscalers or Chinese firms. True sovereignty means choosing dependencies rather than having them imposed.

Articles.Title: Who Writes AI's Rules When Someone Else Owns the Machines?

stories.Headline: EU places ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox under strictest platform rules
stories.Summary:
The European Union has classified ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine and designated Reddit and Roblox as Very Large Online Platforms under its Digital Services Act. These three American companies will now face direct supervision from the European Commission and must comply with stricter requirements designed to address risks related to children, election integrity, and public security. The rules apply to services with over 45 million users in the EU, bringing the total number of regulated platforms to 28.

Companies failing to meet the new requirements within four months face fines up to 6 percent of their annual global revenue. Reddit reported 57.2 million EU users in July, while Roblox has 46.6 million. OpenAI stated it would prepare to meet ChatGPT's additional obligations, and Roblox welcomed the designation, emphasizing safety's importance. This designation adds another regulatory layer for ChatGPT, which already complies with the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act.

stories.Headline: 《TAIPEI TIMES》 Taiwan aims to train 500,000 AI pros by 2040 - 焦點
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's government plans to invest over 40 billion Taiwan dollars, approximately 1.26 billion US dollars, to develop 10 major artificial intelligence projects next year. President William Lai has set an ambitious goal to train at least 500,000 AI professionals by 2040. The administration launched the AI Talent Ark Project this year to nurture talent through fundamental education, professional development, and data-driven approaches, aiming to build a large AI talent pool and strengthen Taiwan's competitiveness in technology sectors.

The government is also prioritizing technological sovereignty and national resilience. The Minister of Digital Affairs announced plans to accumulate at least 10,000 graphics processing units through private investment in AI computing centers within a year. Taiwan is focusing on developing sovereign AI systems that understand Taiwanese perspectives and languages, along with low-Earth-orbit satellite communications to ensure independent communication capabilities. Officials emphasized that technological sovereignty means focusing on critical technologies rather than developing every technology domestically.

stories.Headline: CSA's Top Cloud Threats: Identity, AI -- Campus Technology
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Security Alliance surveyed 507 security professionals to identify the top threats to cloud computing in 2026. Identity and access management issues rose to the number one concern, moving up from second place in 2024, while misconfiguration dropped to fifth. Two artificial intelligence-related threats appeared in the rankings for the first time, including AI-enhanced attacks and AI system compromise. The top eleven threats also include insecure third-party resources, insecure APIs, advanced persistent threats, and inadequate cloud security strategy and governance.

The survey results reveal a significant shift in the cloud threat landscape, with organizations now prioritizing identity protection, artificial intelligence risks, and software supply chains over infrastructure-focused concerns. Security scores ranged closely from 7.95 for identity and access management to 7.45 for system vulnerabilities. The report aims to help organizations make informed risk-management decisions about cloud adoption by providing expert analysis of technical and business impacts, real-world examples, and corresponding security controls across cloud and AI environments.

stories.Headline: AI Now Writes 86% of Paisabazaar's New Code, Reshaping How its Engineers Build Productively and Innovatively
stories.Summary:
Paisabazaar, India's leading financial products marketplace, reports that artificial intelligence now generates approximately 86 percent of new code written on its platform. The company's Chief Technology Officer emphasized that the objective is not to eliminate engineers but to enhance their productivity by automating repetitive tasks. This shift allows engineers to focus on architecture, problem-solving and innovation while accelerating development velocity and enabling teams to pursue a larger product roadmap.

The financial services company is expanding its engineering team despite increased AI involvement, demonstrating its commitment to using productivity gains for expansion rather than workforce reduction. AI-assisted development is integrated throughout the engineering lifecycle, including code writing, testing, debugging and documentation. The company plans to continue deepening AI adoption across both engineering and consumer-facing experiences to expand innovation, improve productivity and deliver more personalized financial services at scale.

stories.Headline: OptiValue Tek Eyes Next Phase of Growth, Expands Focus on AI, Digital Twins and Defence Technology
stories.Summary:
OptiValue Tek Consulting Limited, a New Delhi-based technology company, is moving into a new growth phase with increased emphasis on artificial intelligence, digital twins, and defence technology. The firm has launched ICUDS, an AI-powered counter-drone platform designed to protect critical infrastructure through detection and tracking capabilities. The company received a multi-million-dollar government order through India's Government e-Marketplace to support this expansion. OptiValue is broadening its reach into defence, energy, manufacturing, and logistics sectors as organizations seek better decision-making tools.

The company is also developing digital twins, which create virtual replicas of physical systems to test scenarios and identify vulnerabilities before real-world problems occur. To support this strategy, OptiValue has formed partnerships with Eagle Infrastructure India for intelligent infrastructure development and with SFJ Business Solutions for AI transformation programmes. Chairman Ashish Kumar emphasized the company's goal to connect artificial intelligence with physical systems across defence and critical infrastructure, positioning digital twins as a bridge between digital engineering and operational intelligence for improved organizational resilience.

stories.Headline: Brazil archbishop establishes rules for use of AI in archdiocesan communications
stories.Summary:
Archbishop Josafá Menezes da Silva of Aracaju, Brazil has created guidelines for artificial intelligence use within his archdiocese. The rules require all AI-generated content to undergo human review before publication and to be clearly labeled to distinguish it from human-created work. The archbishop based these directives on Church teachings about human dignity and Pope Leo XIV's messages about AI's potential to create false realities and deepfakes.

The guidelines prohibit clergy from using AI to recreate their appearance, voice, or simulate statements they never made. However, AI can serve as an auxiliary tool for creating backgrounds, textures, illustrations, and assisting with visual composition. The archbishop emphasized that all Church communications must remain truthful and responsible, urging pastoral workers and the faithful to consult with church leadership when using technology to ensure it serves the Church's mission.

stories.Headline: China promotes coordinated development of data industry, artificial intelligence-- Beijing Review
stories.Summary:
# Summary

China's data industry reached 6.78 trillion yuan in 2025, and the country is now focusing on coordinating development between its data sector and artificial intelligence capabilities. The 2026 China International Big Data Industry Expo, held in Guiyang from August 28-30, attracted 372 companies and over 16,000 guests to showcase innovations in computing power, large models, and data circulation. Government officials emphasized that high-quality datasets are essential for advancing AI capabilities and that data technology is transforming traditional industries like power generation and renewable energy forecasting.

Beyond upgrading existing industries, data and AI are creating new business opportunities and employment categories. Companies are hiring data collectors to train robots through embodied intelligence projects, while micro-enterprises and one-person startups are emerging as signs of entrepreneurial growth. International participants from Zimbabwe, Chile, Pakistan, and other nations attended to explore cooperation opportunities, with officials highlighting the potential for shared benefits and technological exchange between countries through collaborative data and AI development.

stories.Headline: The S&P 500 Has Fallen in 56% of Septembers Since 1928. Here's What That Means for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks.
stories.Summary:
Historical data shows that the S&P 500 has fallen in 56% of Septembers since 1928, with an average decline of about 1.17% during that month. This pattern, known as the September Effect, may stem from psychological expectations, investor profit-taking, tax-loss harvesting strategies, and major Federal Reserve decisions that typically occur in September. However, the market has risen in 44% of Septembers, and the average declines are relatively modest.

Despite potential September volatility affecting the broader market, artificial intelligence stocks like Nvidia and Micron Technology remain strong investments. Nvidia recently reported revenues that more than doubled year-over-year to $96.2 billion, with management forecasting 70% revenue growth ahead. Micron is also performing strongly and reports earnings in late September. Both companies are leaders in the AI infrastructure sector, with tech companies expected to spend $1.3 trillion on data center buildouts next year, suggesting that any September price declines in these stocks could present buying opportunities for investors.
